description: We're data people: a physics-trained data scientist who worked on Mayak, a crowdfunded satellite launched in 2017, and a data engineer. We want to use machine learning to find patterns in NASA's microgravity combustion data.
summary:
We developed an open dataset of every test recorded in the run tables of NASA PSI's combustion investigations, with every value traced to its NASA file and row, presented in a dashboard with an oxygen-vs-pressure map, transparent rankings of all 24 investigations for a Moon Base and a spacecraft, investigation profiles, a comparison view, an Earth-vs-orbit comparison, and downloads.

We chose a dataset rather than a predictive model on purpose: in PSI, no fabric or plastic has burned above 22.7% oxygen, so any model of flammability at 30%+ would be guessing beyond the data. In fire safety that is risky. Mapping the evidence first shows where it is solid and where it is missing.

It addresses the challenge by showing where fire-safety evidence exists and where tests are needed before crews live at 30%+ oxygen. The dataset is open (CC0) and reproducible, and from February 2027 a GitHub Actions workflow will refresh it weekly.
details:
What it does and how it works
Moon Base Fire Evidence turns NASA's scattered microgravity fire results into one open, searchable dataset. Python scripts download each combustion investigation's record and official "Experimental table" from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository. They put every test into one table with common columns (fuel, oxygen, pressure, airflow, diluent gas, outcome) and record the exact source file and row for every value. Values are copied or unit-converted, never estimated; anything we had to interpret is flagged in the data.

The dashboard built on it:

  • maps all 1,984 tests by oxygen and pressure against the Moon Base target (≥30% O₂, ≤10.2 psi)
  • ranks all 24 investigations for a Moon Base and for a spacecraft with a transparent score (what burned, fire-safety role, atmosphere match, amount of data), showing the reason for every point
  • profiles each investigation: fuels and sample shapes, conditions, what varied, sensors, fire-safety meaning, Earth applications
  • compares investigations side by side, shows PSI's only sample-by-sample Earth-vs-orbit comparison (Saffire-II), and offers every table for download

Benefits
Researchers and engineers can see in minutes what took us days to assemble: which conditions have been tested in orbit, which materials, and where. Every number links back to NASA's own file, so it can be checked and cited.

Intended impact
It shows where fire-safety evidence for a 30%+ oxygen Moon Base exists and where it is missing. In PSI, no fabric or plastic has burned above 22.7% O₂, and only 20 tests (all gas flames) fall in Moon Base conditions. NASA's Saffire-VI did burn fabric at 31% O₂, but that data isn't in PSI yet. Making these gaps visible helps decide which tests to run before crews live in that atmosphere.

Tools
Python (requests, openpyxl) for downloading and parsing; HTML and JavaScript for the dashboard, with no libraries; GitHub and GitHub Pages for open hosting; a weekly GitHub Actions workflow (from February 2027) that rebuilds the dataset from NASA's sources; Claude (Anthropic) as an SI tool. Code is MIT-licensed and the data is CC0.

What's creative
Instead of a model trained on thin data, we built the evidence map first and made the ranking fully transparent, so anyone can see why an investigation scores high and re-weight it. The chart also shows what is not in the archive: NASA's newer Saffire-VI burns are drawn as reference points outside the PSI count.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: no estimated values; every interpretation flagged; claims limited to what PSI contains.
  • Scope: inverse flames are excluded from Moon Base counts, because their oxygen value is the burner stream, not the cabin air.
  • Longevity: an open, reproducible dataset that grows as NASA adds Saffire IV–VI, SoFIE, LUCI and FM2 data.
  • Safety: this maps evidence; it does not certify materials or predict fires.
